title: Super-exponential anticoncentration of the random ±1 permanent at zero
credit: Conjecture 6.12 in V. Vu's survey (arXiv:2005.02797); current bound Hunter-Kwan-Sauermann (arXiv:2509.22577).
premise_risks: Attributed to Vu ('as conjectured by Vu'); appears unnamed as 'Conjecture 6.12 (Permanent)' but the owner may count it as person-attributed
Hunter-Kwan-Sauermann is a 2025 arXiv preprint (refereeing status unknown); the claim does not depend on it beyond context
plain: Fill an n by n matrix with independent random signs +1/-1 and compute its permanent (the determinant without the minus signs). The chance that the determinant is 0 is about 2^(-n), mostly because two rows or columns can be equal or opposite. The permanent has no such structural reason to vanish, and in 2025 its chance of being 0 was shown to be exponentially small. Is it super-exponentially small, that is, smaller than e^(-Cn) for every fixed C once n is large?
math: Let $p_n=2^{-n^2}\,\#\{M\in\{\pm1\}^{n\times n}:\operatorname{per}M=0\}$, where $\operatorname{per}M=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n M_{i\pi(i)}$. Prove or disprove: for every $C>0$ there is $N$ such that $p_n\le e^{-Cn}$ for all $n\ge N$ (equivalently $\tfrac1n\log p_n\to-\infty$, with $\log 0=-\infty$). Known: $p_n\le e^{-cn}$ for some absolute $c>0$.
